newsitem.title: JAPAN: N.Korea to attend briefing on peace talks.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea to attend briefing on peace talks.

text.p: North Korea on Friday announced it will attend a briefing with the United States and South Korea on Korean peace talks, a sign the communist North was trying to put on a normal face after an embarassing high-level defection.
In a brief statement by the Foreign Ministry, Pyongyang said it would attend the U.S.-South Korean briefing in New York on March 5 to discuss four-way peace talks involving China.
North Korea twice delayed the talks earlier this month in what was seen as an effort to press Washington to provide more food aid for its hungry population.
The United States insists it never promised Pyongyang a specific amount of food aid in return for North Korea's participation in the briefing.

The four-way talks were proposed last April by Washington and Seoul to defuse tensions -- and eventually bring about a permanent peace -- on the Korean peninsula, which was divided in the 1950-53 Korean War. The two Koreas remain technically at war since the conflict ended in a truce and not a peace pact.
Earlier on Friday, North Korea announced the appointment of an acting premier to replace Kang Song-san, the sixth-ranked official in its power structure.

The news set off new speculation about turmoil in North Korea's leadership since Hwang Jang-yop's defection in Beijing on February 12. Hwang, the country's 24th-ranked official, was a close adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.
A report on Pyongyang Radio said Deputy Prime Minister Hong Song-nam had been appointed acting premier.

The report, monitored by the Tokyo-based news agency Radiopress, which follows North Korea's media, gave no reason why Hong, 73, was taking over the post of premier. Kang, 66, had held the post since December 1992.
But Radiopress analyst Noriyuki Suzuki said Kang had not been seen in public since January 1996 and speculated that the health of the long-time diabetic had deteriorated.
In Seoul, a senior official of the National Unification Ministry also said Kang had not appeared in public for a year because of illness.
Other analysts said the timing of the appointment could be a clue to other factors.

"I believe the change has something to do with Kang's health, but the question is why is the appointment being announced now," said Masao Okonogi, professor of Korean history at Tokyo's Keio University.
"We can't rule out other possibilities, such as a leadership purge connected with Hwang's defection," he told Reuters.
Kang, like Hwang, supported an opening of the Stalinist nation to economic reforms to save it from collapse. Two years of devastating floods have set off widespread famine.

Kang was among seven senior North Korean officials thought to be politically close to Hwang and therefore likely targets of an impending purge by a hard-line group headed by de facto leader Kim Jong-il, said Modern Korea Institute Director Katsumi Sato.
"If Kim's group fails to purge the reformers, it will give the impression that they lack the power to do so, and that would trigger a stampede to the reformist camp," he said.
Suzuki said Kang ranked sixth in North Korea's power structure while Hong, a vice premier since October 1987 and a Politburo alternate member since March 1989, ranked 19th.
Suzuki said Hong, expected to be confirmed as permanent premier once North Korea's parliament convenes after a three-year recess, has close ties with the Chinese leadership.
In May 1996 he led a North Korean delegation to Beijing, where he met Prime Minister Li Peng and won a pledge of 20,000 tonnes of badly needed food aid.
